article.title: ESLint Adds an Official Shell Script Linting Plugin, Extending Its Language-Agnostic Platform
article.summary: ESLint introduced @eslint/shell, an officially supported plugin that lints Bash, POSIX sh and mksh scripts with rules inspired by ShellCheck.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

ESLint now officially supports linting shell scripts. According to [ESLint's announcement](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/), the project introduced the `@eslint/shell` plugin on November 6, giving the JavaScript-ecosystem linter the ability to check Bash, POSIX `sh` and MirBSD Korn shell (mksh) scripts alongside the JavaScript, JSON, Markdown and CSS files it already handles.

## What We Know

The new plugin extends a multi-year push to turn ESLint into a general-purpose tool rather than a JavaScript-only one. [ESLint's announcement](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/) says the project "announced our plan to make ESLint a more general-purpose linter capable of linting any language" back in July 2024, and that it has "added official support for JSON, Markdown, and CSS" since then. The shell plugin is presented as the next addition to that list, not a replacement for any of the earlier ones.

`@eslint/shell` is described in [ESLint's announcement](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/) as providing "parsing for shell scripts, a set of rules inspired by ShellCheck checks, and a recommended configuration." [ShellCheck](https://www.shellcheck.net/) is an existing, independently maintained tool that "finds bugs in your shell scripts," and ESLint's new rule set draws on the kinds of problems it already catches rather than inventing a new rule taxonomy from scratch.

The plugin covers three shell dialects. Per [ESLint's announcement](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/), it "supports Bash, POSIX `sh`, and MirBSD Korn shell (mksh)," and the [plugin's GitHub repository](https://github.com/eslint/shell) names these as separate language implementations — `shell/bash`, `shell/posix` and `shell/mksh`. The recommended configuration defaults to Bash; manual configuration lets a project pick a different dialect. ESLint's announcement says the default configuration "enables rules catching common problems, such as unquoted expansions, unused variables, and unsafe `read` usage," and that the rule set more broadly "cover[s] issues including legacy command substitutions, iterating over `ls` output, unquoted expansions, and variables in `printf` format strings."

Under the hood, the plugin parses scripts into what [ESLint's announcement](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/) calls an "ESTree-style syntax tree," the same tree format ESLint's JavaScript rules traverse, which is what lets shell-script linting plug into ESLint's existing rule-execution and configuration machinery. ESLint says the parser underneath "is built on `mvdan-sh`, the parser used by `shfmt`" — a reference to an existing, independently maintained project. According to [the mvdan/sh GitHub repository](https://github.com/mvdan/sh), that project is "a shell parser, formatter, and interpreter" supporting POSIX Shell, Bash, Zsh and mksh, and shfmt is "the formatting utility bundled with this project," used to standardize shell script formatting. ESLint's announcement adds that the resulting shell syntax tree can be inspected directly in the ESLint Code Explorer.

Installation follows ESLint's normal plugin pattern. The [`@eslint/shell` repository](https://github.com/eslint/shell) lists the install command as `npm install --save-dev eslint @eslint/shell`, and states the plugin requires Node.js `^20.19.0 || ^22.13.0 || >=24` and has been tested against ESLint v10. The repository lists the plugin under an Apache-2.0 license.

## What We Don't Know

ESLint's announcement does not give adoption figures, a version number tied specifically to this launch, or a timeline for adding further rules beyond the categories it names. None of the sources consulted for this article state whether `@eslint/shell` rules will be bundled into ESLint's own default configurations for projects that already lint shell scripts via other tools, such as ShellCheck run directly in CI.

## Why It Matters

For projects that already run ESLint across a JavaScript or TypeScript codebase, the new plugin means shell scripts checked into the same repository — build scripts, CI helpers, deployment wrappers — can be linted through the same configuration system and tooling, rather than requiring a separate ShellCheck invocation. [ESLint's announcement](https://eslint.org/blog/2026/11/eslint-shell-plugin-announcement/) frames this directly: "Shell scripts are an important part of many projects. With `@eslint/shell`, users can lint shell scripts alongside other code using ESLint's configuration system."
